Sunlight looks white, but it's actually a mix of all the colors of the rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. You can see this when light passes through a prism or raindrops and splits apart.

Each color travels as a wave, and the waves come in different sizes. Red light has long, lazy waves, while blue and violet light have short, choppy ones.

Our air is made of tiny molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen, far too small to see. When sunlight hits them, the light bounces off in all directions. This is called **scattering**. The short blue waves get scattered much more than the long red waves, about five times more! So blue light gets bounced all over the sky, and wherever you look, some of it is heading toward your eyes. That's why the whole sky glows blue.

But wait, violet waves are even shorter. Why isn't the sky purple? The sun gives off less violet light, and our eyes are much better at seeing blue.

At sunset, sunlight travels through much more air to reach you. By then, most of the blue has been scattered away, leaving the reds and oranges that paint the evening sky.

Have you ever wondered why the sky looks blue instead of purple, green, or plain black? The answer starts with sunlight.

Sunlight looks white, but it is actually a mix of all the colors of the rainbow. Each color travels as a wave, and the waves come in different sizes. Red light has long, lazy waves. Blue and violet light have short, choppy waves.

When sunlight enters our atmosphere, it crashes into tiny gas molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules are much smaller than the light waves. Because of their size, they scatter short waves far more than long ones. Blue light gets bounced around in every direction, bouncing from molecule to molecule all across the sky. Red and yellow light mostly pass straight through. Scientists call this Rayleigh scattering.

So when you look up, blue light is reaching your eyes from every part of the sky at once.

But wait: violet waves are even shorter. Why isn't the sky violet? Partly because the Sun gives off less violet light, and partly because our eyes are much more sensitive to blue.

At sunset, sunlight travels through more air to reach you. Most of the blue scatters away before it arrives, leaving those gorgeous reds and oranges behind.

## How a Browser Cache Works

When you visit a website, your browser downloads files such as images, logos, stylesheets (which control how the page looks), and scripts (which make it interactive). Downloading these takes time and data. To speed things up, your browser saves copies of many of these files on your computer. This storage area is called the **cache**.

Think of it like keeping a cookbook on your kitchen shelf instead of walking to the library every time you want a recipe. The next time you visit the same site, your browser checks its cache first. If it already has a file, it can load it instantly from your computer instead of downloading it again. That's why websites often load faster on your second visit.

But what if the website changes? Websites send instructions along with their files, telling the browser how long to keep each one. A logo might be kept for months, while a news headline might be refreshed every few minutes. When a file "expires," the browser asks the website for a fresh copy.

Sometimes the cache holds outdated files, causing a page to look broken or old. That's why "clear your cache" is common troubleshooting advice. It forces the browser to download everything fresh.

**How a Browser Cache Works**

Imagine you visit your favorite news website. Your browser has to download many pieces to show you that page: text, images, logos, fonts, and code files. Downloading all of this takes time and uses your internet connection.

A browser cache is like a small storage closet on your own computer. The first time you visit a website, your browser saves copies of some of those pieces in this closet. The next time you visit, the browser checks the closet first. If it finds a saved copy, it uses that instead of downloading the file again. This makes pages load much faster.

Websites decide how long their files should stay in the cache. A company logo might stay for months because it rarely changes. A news headline might expire quickly because it updates often. When a saved file gets too old, the browser asks the website for a fresh version.

Caching has clear benefits: faster loading, less data usage, and less work for website servers.

Sometimes, though, the cache causes problems. You might see an outdated version of a page. That is why people often suggest "clearing your cache." This empties the closet, forcing your browser to download everything fresh.

Don't compare your chapter one to someone else's chapter twenty. Build tiny things. Celebrate small wins. Google shamelessly. Ask questions without apology.

The phone was ringing when Agnes found it, which was the first wrong thing.

The second was that it was dry. She had come down the cliff path at first light, as she did every morning after a storm, to check the rocks for whatever the sea had decided to return: rope, plastic crates, once a child's shoe that she still kept on the windowsill and did not like to think about. The tide had gone out an hour before. Kelp lay in black ropes over the stones, and everything glistened, everything dripped, except the phone, which sat on a flat shelf of granite as if someone had set it down to answer the door.

It was an old thing, beige, with a coiled cord that ran into a crack in the rock and disappeared. Not a mobile. A proper telephone, the kind that had hung on the kitchen wall in her mother's house.

It rang again. The sound was thin and polite against the wind.

Agnes had kept the Carrick Head light for nineteen years. She knew there was no line out here. She had petitioned for one twice.

She looked back at the tower, its lamp still turning, pale against the morning. Then she picked up the receiver.

The phone was ringing when Elias Marr found it, which was the first wrong thing.

He had gone down to the rocks at dawn the way he always did after a storm, checking for driftwood, for the bodies of gulls, for anything the sea had decided it no longer wanted. The tide had pulled back and left the shelf of black stone gleaming like the skin of some enormous animal. Kelp lay in heaps. A plastic crate. A single boot, laceless and full of sand.

And there, wedged in a crack above the waterline, a telephone.

Not a mobile. A proper telephone, the heavy kind his mother had kept on the hall table, cream colored with a rotary dial and a coiled cord that ran down into the rock and simply disappeared. The bell inside it was trilling, bright and insistent, cutting through the wind as if it had every right to be there.

Elias stood very still. For thirty years he had kept the light on Carrick Point. He knew every sound this island could make. This was not one of them.

The phone rang again.

He told himself he would not answer it. Then he knelt on the wet stone, and he lifted the receiver.

One year ago, I traded my IDE for 1:1s. Here's what my first year as an engineering manager taught me:

**1. Your output is now your team's output.** I used to measure my day in merged PRs. Now a good day might be unblocking three people and writing zero code. That took months to feel okay.

**2. Clarity is kindness.** Vague feedback helps no one. The most respectful thing I can do is be direct, specific, and timely.

**3. Listen more than you talk.** My best 1:1s were the ones where I said the least.

**4. You'll get it wrong, so own it.** I mishandled a reorg conversation early on. Admitting it built more trust than pretending I had it figured out.

**5. Protect your team's focus.** Saying "no" to good ideas is part of the job.

**The Great Gatsby by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)**

Set during the summer of 1922, the novel is narrated by Nick Carraway, a young Midwesterner who moves to West Egg, Long Island, to work in bonds. His mysterious neighbor, Jay Gatsby, throws extravagant parties hoping to attract Daisy Buchanan, Nick's cousin and Gatsby's former love. Daisy is now married to Tom, a wealthy, brutish man having an affair with Myrtle Wilson, the wife of a struggling mechanic. Nick arranges a reunion between Gatsby and Daisy, and their romance rekindles. But tensions explode during a confrontation in a Manhattan hotel, where Daisy ultimately retreats to Tom. Driving home in Gatsby's car, Daisy strikes and kills Myrtle. Gatsby shields her, and Tom lets Myrtle's grieving husband believe Gatsby was responsible. Wilson shoots Gatsby, then himself. Almost no one attends Gatsby's funeral, and a disillusioned Nick returns west.

Thematically, the novel critiques the American Dream, suggesting that the pursuit of wealth and reinvention can be hollow and corrupting. Gatsby's longing for Daisy, symbolized by the green light across the bay, represents the impossibility of recapturing the past. Fitzgerald also exposes the moral carelessness of the rich, rigid class divisions, and the spiritual emptiness behind the Jazz Age's glittering excess.

**Frankenstein by Mary Shelley (1818)**

Mary Shelley's *Frankenstein* follows Victor Frankenstein, a gifted young scientist obsessed with discovering the secret of life. After years of feverish study, he assembles a creature from dead body parts and brings it to life. Horrified by its appearance, Victor abandons his creation immediately.

Alone and rejected, the creature educates itself by secretly observing a family of cottagers. It learns language, reads literature, and longs for companionship. When the family discovers it and flees in terror, the creature's loneliness turns to rage. It seeks out Victor and demands a female companion. Victor begins the task but destroys the unfinished mate, fearing the consequences. In revenge, the creature murders Victor's loved ones, including his bride, Elizabeth. Victor pursues the creature to the Arctic, where he dies aboard an explorer's ship. The grieving creature vows to end its own life.

The novel explores the dangers of unchecked ambition and the ethical limits of scientific discovery. It also examines responsibility, asking what creators owe to what they create. Shelley suggests that monstrousness is shaped by neglect and isolation rather than inborn nature. Ultimately, the story questions who the true monster is: the creature or the man who abandoned it.

Johannes Gutenberg's movable-type printing press, developed around 1440, transformed Europe by making information cheap, fast, and widely available. Before printing, books were copied by hand, usually by monks, which made them rare, expensive, and prone to errors. Within decades of Gutenberg's invention, presses spread to hundreds of cities, and millions of books circulated across the continent.

This explosion of printed material reshaped religion. Martin Luther used pamphlets to spread his criticisms of the Catholic Church rapidly, fueling the Protestant Reformation. Bibles printed in vernacular languages allowed ordinary people to read scripture themselves, weakening the Church's control over interpretation.

The press also accelerated the Scientific Revolution. Scholars could share discoveries accurately and build on one another's work, as with Copernicus's and Vesalius's influential texts. Standardized editions reduced copying mistakes and helped knowledge accumulate rather than degrade.

Literacy rose as books became affordable, and printing in local languages helped standardize them, strengthening emerging national identities. Newspapers and political pamphlets later encouraged public debate, laying groundwork for the Enlightenment and challenges to absolute authority.

In short, the printing press democratized knowledge, breaking elite monopolies on information and setting Europe on a path toward modern science, religious pluralism, and political change.

Martin Luther's ideas spread with astonishing speed in 1517 because pamphlets could be printed by the thousands, helping launch the Protestant Reformation and weakening the authority of the Catholic Church. Today we are excited to announce one of our most requested features: Inkwell now syncs edits you make while offline.

Whether you are on a flight, riding the subway, or working from a cabin with spotty Wi-Fi, you can keep writing without interruption. Create new notes, edit existing ones, add checklists, and reorganize folders just as you normally would. Every change is saved securely on your device.

The moment you reconnect, Inkwell automatically syncs your updates across all your devices. There is nothing to tap and nothing to remember. Your phone, tablet, and laptop will all show the latest version within seconds.

What if you edited the same note on two devices while offline? Our new smart merge system combines changes line by line whenever possible. If two edits truly conflict, Inkwell keeps both versions side by side so you can choose what stays. Nothing you write is ever lost.

Offline sync is available today for all users on iOS, Android, Mac, and Windows. Simply update to the latest version of the app to get started.

We built this because your ideas should never wait for a signal. Thank you for your feedback, and happy writing!

**Rain, Chowder, and Cable Cars: San Francisco's Secret Side**

I had planned a sunny stroll across the Golden Gate Bridge, but San Francisco had other ideas. By mid-morning, a steady rain swept in off the Pacific, turning the city's famous hills into glistening ribbons of gray. Instead of fighting it, I surrendered. I ducked into a tiny café in North Beach, where the espresso machine hissed like a friendly cat and the windows fogged with the warmth of strangers sheltering together. Later, I rode a cable car up Powell Street, the gripman ringing his bell as raindrops streaked sideways past the open benches. Locals barely flinched; here, weather is less an inconvenience than a mood. I wandered through City Lights Bookstore, losing an hour among Beat poetry and the comforting smell of old paper. By afternoon, the clouds thinned just enough to reveal Alcatraz floating in a silver haze, mysterious and moody across the bay. I ended the day at the Ferry Building, slurping clam chowder from a sourdough bowl while the rain drummed softly on the roof. San Francisco in sunshine is beautiful, but San Francisco in the rain feels intimate, like the city is quietly sharing a secret that only those who linger long enough will hear.

The rain arrived before I did, slipping over the Golden Gate in soft gray sheets while the city was still yawning awake. San Francisco on a wet morning feels like a secret shared only with locals and the brave. I ducked into a tiny cafe in the Mission, where the windows fogged and the barista handed me a cortado with a knowing smile, as if to say I had chosen the right day to wander. By noon, the cable cars were clanging through puddles on Powell Street, their wooden benches slick and gleaming. I rode one anyway, clutching the brass pole as raindrops stung my cheeks and the hills dropped away toward the bay. Chinatown glowed beneath strings of red lanterns, the colors deepened by the damp, and the scent of roasting pork drifted from open doorways. Later, I sheltered inside City Lights Bookstore, losing an hour among poetry shelves while rain drummed on the roof. As evening settled in, the fog swallowed Coit Tower and the streetlights shimmered on wet pavement like scattered coins. I walked back to my hotel soaked, happy, and certain that this famously moody city shows its truest heart when the sky decides to weep.

**Hikari Ramen: Worth the Wait (Barely)**
★★★½

Let's start with what matters: the broth at Hikari Ramen is extraordinary. Their signature tonkotsu simmers for eighteen hours, and you can taste every minute of it. It's rich, creamy, and deeply porky without ever feeling greasy. A splash of black garlic oil adds smoky depth, while the springy noodles hold up beautifully to the last slurp. The chashu melts on contact.

Unfortunately, getting that bowl in front of you requires patience. On a Tuesday evening with half the tables empty, we waited fifteen minutes just to order and another thirty-five for our food. Water refills never came, and flagging down our server felt like an Olympic event. The staff seemed overwhelmed rather than rude, but that's little comfort when you're starving.

My advice? Come early, bring a friend you enjoy talking to, and don't arrive hungry. The ramen deserves five stars. The service, sadly, does not.

**Worth the Wait, Mostly**

Tucked into a narrow storefront on Maple Street, Kumo Ramen serves the best tonkotsu broth I have tasted outside of Japan. It arrives rich and creamy, simmered for what must be days, with a deep, savory pork flavor balanced by a gentle hint of garlic and sesame. The noodles hold their bite, the chashu melts on the tongue, and the soft egg is perfectly jammy.

Unfortunately, getting that bowl requires serious patience. We waited twenty minutes before anyone took our order, and another thirty passed before our food appeared. The staff seemed overwhelmed rather than careless, rushing between tables with apologetic smiles, but the delays were hard to ignore on a weeknight.

If you have time to spare, Kumo is absolutely worth a visit for the broth alone. Just arrive early, bring good company, and do not come starving, because your stomach will be growling long before the first slurp.

Remote work, for all its genuine benefits, quietly hurts junior engineers more than it helps them, at least when companies treat it as a simple change of location rather than a change in how teams operate. Early in a career, much of the most valuable learning is accidental: overhearing a senior colleague debug a production outage, catching a quick whiteboard sketch of the system architecture, or asking a "dumb" question over a desk partition without feeling like an interruption. Remote setups strip away these moments, replacing them with scheduled calls and Slack threads that juniors often hesitate to start. The result is slower skill growth, weaker professional networks, and a tendency to struggle silently for hours on problems a mentor could resolve in minutes. Visibility suffers too; quiet competence is easy to overlook when your manager sees you only as a square on a screen. That said, remote work is not inherently harmful. Teams that invest in deliberate mentorship, frequent pairing sessions, documented decisions, and explicit permission to ask questions can give juniors an even richer experience than a distracted open office. The problem is not distance itself, but the lazy assumption that learning will simply happen on its own.

Remote work, for all its benefits, quietly hurts most junior engineers, and companies should stop pretending otherwise. Early in a career, the most valuable learning rarely happens in scheduled meetings or formal documentation. It happens when a new developer overhears a senior colleague debugging a production outage, asks a quick question at someone's desk, or watches how experienced teammates negotiate tradeoffs in real time. These small, unplanned moments compound into judgment, which is the skill that separates competent engineers from great ones. Remote setups strip most of that away. Juniors often hesitate to message busy coworkers on Slack, worried about seeming incompetent, so they spin their wheels for hours on problems a mentor could solve in minutes. Their work also becomes less visible, which makes it harder to earn trust, stretch assignments, and promotions. Seasoned engineers, by contrast, already have the networks and instincts to thrive at home. None of this means remote work is doomed. Teams can offset the damage with deliberate pairing sessions, generous office hours, and explicit norms that reward asking questions. But without that intentional effort, remote work widens the gap between those who already know and those still learning, and juniors pay the price.

Running and swimming are both excellent cardiovascular exercises, but they suit different needs and lifestyles.

**Running** is highly accessible. All you need is a good pair of shoes, and you can do it almost anywhere, anytime. It burns a large number of calories, strengthens the legs and core, and, as a weight-bearing activity, helps build bone density. However, the repeated impact can stress the knees, hips, and ankles, making injuries like shin splints or runner's knee fairly common, especially for beginners or heavier individuals.

**Swimming**, by contrast, is low-impact. The water supports your body weight, which makes it ideal for people with joint problems, injuries, or arthritis. It works nearly every major muscle group, including the arms, shoulders, back, and legs, providing a more balanced full-body workout. Swimming also improves lung capacity and flexibility. Its drawbacks are practical: you need access to a pool or safe open water, proper technique takes time to learn, and it does less for bone density.

Ultimately, the better choice depends on your goals and circumstances. Running offers convenience and bone-strengthening benefits, while swimming provides gentle, comprehensive conditioning. Many fitness experts recommend combining both, using swimming as a recovery or cross-training activity to balance running's high impact.

Running and swimming are both excellent ways to build cardiovascular fitness, but they offer different benefits and challenges.

Running is highly accessible. All you need is a good pair of shoes and a safe route, and you can head out almost anywhere at any time. It burns a large number of calories per hour and, because it is weight bearing, helps strengthen bones and lower body muscles. However, the repeated pounding can strain joints, shins, and knees, making injuries fairly common, especially for beginners or heavier individuals.

Swimming, by contrast, is gentle on the body. Water supports your weight, so it places very little stress on joints. This makes it ideal for people recovering from injury, older adults, or anyone with arthritis. It also works the entire body, engaging the arms, shoulders, back, core, and legs at once. The main drawbacks are access and skill. You need a pool or safe open water, and proper technique takes time to learn. Swimming also does less to build bone density.

Ultimately, the best choice depends on your goals, body, and lifestyle. Many people find that combining both activities offers balanced fitness, variety, and a lower risk of overuse injuries.

Clever code feels great to write. Simple code feels great to read six months later at 2am when production is down. Guess which one matters more. 🧵

2/
Code is read far more often than it's written. Every "clever" one-liner is a puzzle you force your teammates (and future you) to solve before they can change anything. That cost adds up with every read.

3/
Debugging is harder than writing. As Kernighan put it: if you write code as cleverly as possible, you are by definition not smart enough to debug it. Leave yourself some headroom.

4/
Simple code is easier to test, review, refactor, and hand off. Clever code tends to hide assumptions, edge cases, and bugs behind elegance. Boring code puts everything in plain sight.

5/
Before you commit, ask: "Could a new teammate understand this in 30 seconds?" If not, simplify. Clear names, obvious flow, no magic. The best code isn't impressive. It's unsurprising. ✅

1/5
Clever code feels great to write. You squeeze 20 lines into one, use a trick nobody else knows, and feel like a wizard. Then six months pass, and you're the one staring at it, confused. Here's why simple code wins almost every time. 🧵

2/5
Code is read far more often than it's written. Every teammate who touches your code pays a "cleverness tax" to understand it. Simple code lets people grasp intent in seconds instead of minutes. Readability is a feature, not a luxury.

3/5
Bugs love to hide in clever code. When logic is dense and tricky, edge cases slip through unnoticed. Simple, explicit code makes mistakes obvious. If you can't easily explain what a line does, you probably can't easily test it either.

4/5
Simple code is easier to change. Requirements always shift. A straightforward function can be extended, refactored, or deleted with confidence. A clever one often has to be fully decoded before anyone dares to modify it, and that slows the whole team down.

5/5
The real skill isn't writing code only you understand. It's solving hard problems in ways anyone can follow. As Brian Kernighan put it, debugging is twice as hard as writing code, so if you write it as cleverly as possible, you can't debug it. Keep it simple. 💡
